name: Yara Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential; you can tell me what you say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead three clerks on disputed motor and home claims at Marlow Mutual. I read the policy wording, chase missing repair photos and call people when a refusal needs explaining. I like finding the small clause that fixes a real mistake, though the queue grows whenever somebody leaves. I've never used an AI tool, and I don't want a wrong refusal under my name.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the day stays with you after you go home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Last month our manager left a claims desk empty after a contract ended, and I took its hardest files home in my head. I have a bachelor's degree and about three months of rent and bills saved. Leila, my partner, works steady library hours, but our flat needs both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the claims team that AI Plateau means our basic checks and pay stay much the same. A quicker form search would be useful, but a policy still needs a person who knows what the words mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't think our branch is as steady as people say. A cancelled motor policy last month led my manager to leave a vacant desk empty, and my three months of savings would go quickly if that became a habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep checking disputed claims and train the two newer clerks on the paper trail this quarter. I'll also put 80 from each monthly pay cheque into savings until I have four months of rent and bills; I won't buy an AI subscription I don't know how to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm mostly settled at work, though that empty desk nags at me. I can meet my rent now, and another insurer across town hires occasionally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you the empty desk is a real problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd notice is another pile of claims on Monday morning because nobody filled the desk. I'd ask my manager whether the vacancy is being advertised before I decide there's a threat to my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or plan changes if it does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Leila and I can skip two weekend trips without making life miserable. An empty desk at the insurer can become a smaller payslip long before a clever machine arrives.

say: I'd say **AI Plateau** leaves claims checks and wages mostly as they are.
I'd welcome a **faster form search** while keeping a person on disputed cases.
think: I worry the **unfilled desk** means the branch may trim staff for ordinary business reasons.
My **three-month cushion** would disappear quickly if my pay stopped.
do: Keep **checking disputed claims** and coach two newer clerks this quarter.
Save **80 each month** toward four months of rent and bills.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a nagging worry about the branch vacancy.
S0.quote: An empty desk at the insurer can become a smaller payslip long before a clever machine arrives.
fieldNote: She links risk to an **unfilled vacancy**, not the small AI change.
She refuses an **AI subscription** until she sees a work use.
The four-month savings goal gives her a **small test** she can control this year.

steps.text: Keep checking disputed insurance claims and coach two new clerks
Save 80 from each monthly cheque for rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say Steady Disruption will put claim summaries and policy checks on a screen before it puts robots in the office. I'd ask who checks the software's mistakes when a customer challenges a refusal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see our insurer keeping one senior checker and dropping two junior desks as people leave. I'm good at the exception cases, but I might be told to supervise twice the files for the same pay; that is a real risk to my hours if I refuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask my manager for written figures on new claims targets and whether the empty post will be filled. If the targets rise without paid review time, I'll apply to the mutual insurer across town for a claims appeal role and put 100 a month aside while I'm still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, even though I sound stubborn in the team meeting. The work might stay, but the paid time to do it properly could shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which claim would make a speed target unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rejected flood claim needs the photos, the policy wording and somebody to answer a person who is already upset. I won't sign off on a computer's refusal after a thirty-second glance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want to stay, yet you would apply elsewhere. What decides it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Leila the rent account before we book another trip. If my manager will fund proper review time and keep a named appeal clerk, I could stay; if not, I'll take interviews elsewhere only when there is a real paid vacancy. I would compare the offer after travel costs with our rent and bills before handing in notice.

say: I'd ask who **checks refusals** when software drafts claims decisions.
I'd say robots matter **later** for office work than AI claim summaries.
think: The insurer may let **junior desks** disappear and increase my file load.
I could lose **paid hours** if I resist unsafe speed targets.
do: Ask for **written targets** and paid review time this month.
Apply for a **claims appeal vacancy** only if targets rise without safeguards.
Set aside **100 monthly** while my wages continue.
feel: **Anxious** about hours and the quality of claim decisions.
S1.quote: I won't sign off on a computer's refusal after a thirty-second glance.
fieldNote: Her senior skill protects **appeals work**, but higher targets could cut paid time.
A move depends on a **real paid vacancy**, not a guessed opening.
She asks the **employer directly** for targets rather than seeking outside support.

steps.text: Apply for a paid claims appeal vacancy across town if targets rise
Save 100 each month from current wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my colleagues that AGI by 2028 can read and judge most claim files before a robot ever reaches a desk. The insurer must tell us whose posts it expects to cut, and customers need a way to challenge a machine's decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our branch to cut most clerk posts once thinking AI is cheaper, and my senior title won't save my wage. Robots around 2031 add little to my screen work; the danger is the software in 2028 and a rent payment due every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll get the insurer's written redundancy terms and check the benefit rules with the workers' advice centre. I'll stop the weekend trips and put every spare 120 a month into the rent account; I'll also apply for advertised human claims appeal work, but only count an offer if it has paid hours. Before accepting an appeal job I would check take-home pay after the cross-town fare against our rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This would keep me awake. I picture telling Leila that the branch can run claims without my desk and then counting how many rent payments our savings cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would three months of savings mean in the first week after a cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months of expenses is about three rent dates, not a new career. I'd pay rent first and cut travel, and I would not borrow money for an untested course while the pay cheque is in doubt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of help would actually change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a funded place with paid time in a regulated complaints team, if that team still employs people. A promise of 'human oversight' without wages and a vacancy wouldn't help us pay the rent.

say: I'd demand clear **staff-cut plans** and a way to appeal machine claim decisions.
I'd explain that **thinking AI in 2028** reaches our desks before robots around 2031.
think: I expect **most clerk posts** at my branch to go, including mine.
My **three-month savings** cannot bridge an open-ended loss of wages.
do: Get **redundancy terms** and check benefit rules tomorrow.
Cut **weekend trips** and save another 120 monthly while employed.
Apply only for **advertised paid appeals work** with real hours.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep over rent and expected job loss.
S2.quote: Three months of expenses is about three rent dates, not a new career.
fieldNote: She expects a **major personal wage loss**, not merely sector disruption.
**Paid time**, funding and a real vacancy govern any move into appeals work.
She puts **rent first** and refuses to borrow for an uncertain course.

steps.text: Ask the advice centre about benefits and insurer redundancy terms
Cancel weekend trips to cut the flat budget
Transfer 120 monthly from wages into the rent account
Apply for paid appeals only if pay after fare covers rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to settle who is answerable for a wrong claim decision. The robots would come around 2034, but an insurance desk is mostly reading, checking and answering people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years sounds kinder, yet I still think the insurer will eventually need fewer clerks. I could learn complaints work while I still draw a wage, but I won't pretend a course makes a paid job appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next year I'll ask to shadow the appeals clerk one afternoon a month, if my manager pays for that time. I'll keep 100 a month going into savings and check the mutual insurer's advertised openings each quarter; if paid shadowing is refused, I'll ask the local college about a short complaints course only after I know the fee and timetable. In the first year after AGI reaches claims in 2031, I would keep any paid appeals hours I had secured and check that the take-home pay after travel still covers our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious rather than sleepless today. There is room to test the next job before risking our rent, and that changes the feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn during paid shadowing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the clerk to show me a case where the policy wording and a customer's account do not match. A supervisor's signature needs a person who has read both sides, not someone who merely clicked approve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for a course without giving up rent money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila would want the course fee written beside our savings target. I'd use wages to pay a modest fee only if the course fits around shifts; I would not leave a paid post for a promised appeals opening. The fee would have to fit after rent and bills without taking our emergency savings.

say: I'd call for clear **appeal responsibility** before thinking AI reaches claims in 2031.
I'd remind colleagues that **robots follow around 2034** and change little at a desk.
think: I expect **fewer clerk posts**, even with five years to prepare.
I could pay a **modest course fee** from wages after rent, but I cannot empty our buffer without a paid opening.
do: Request **paid appeals shadowing** one afternoon each month.
Save **100 monthly** while still earning my clerk wage.
Check **advertised appeals vacancies** each quarter before a job move.
feel: **Anxious**, with enough time to test a path while employed.
S3.quote: I won't pretend a course makes a paid job appear.
fieldNote: The extra years let her seek **paid shadowing** without quitting.
She distinguishes **training access** from a real paid opening.
She keeps the **current wage** while looking at fees, shifts and openings.

steps.text: Request one paid afternoon monthly shadowing the claims appeals clerk
Save 100 monthly from current insurance wages
Check mutual insurer appeals vacancies every quarter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the office that AGI by 2036 is a planning date, not a reason to clear our desks this Friday. Robots around 2039 may change deliveries or filing, but our big exposure is the screen work ten years out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have ten years of wages before the thinking work changes completely, and that's a useful stretch. Still, I don't want to turn 37 with no savings and a title that exists only on an old staff chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll stay in claims this year and finish the appeals handbook with the new clerks. Leila and I will move 100 a month into a separate account and review our rent and work choices every birthday; by next spring I'll ask whether the insurer funds a complaints certificate during paid hours. In the first year after 2036, I would keep a paid claims role if one remains and compare any complaints offer after travel costs with our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady with a decade in front of me, though I would not ignore it. The thing that helps is a calendar and a salary, not a speech about being flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at the first birthday review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a date beside the certificate request and ask who signs off on it. If the insurer won't pay for study time, I'll keep my wage and first check what the course costs and whether there are actual complaints vacancies nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid placement to switch fields?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Leila we can keep the flat this year and still save for a different route. I won't trade ten years of certain pay for an unpaid placement someone says might become a job.

say: I'd call **2036 a planning date**, while keeping claims work moving now.
I'd say **robots around 2039** matter less to my desk than thinking AI.
think: I could have **ten more years** of wages to build a buffer.
I fear reaching 37 with **outdated skills** and too little saved.
do: Finish the **appeals handbook** with new clerks this year.
Move **100 monthly** into a separate savings account.
Ask about a **paid complaints certificate** by next spring.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with a reason to keep a yearly check.
S4.quote: I won't trade ten years of certain pay for an unpaid placement someone says might become a job.
fieldNote: She uses the **ten-year horizon** for a yearly savings and skills review.
She rejects an **unpaid placement** without evidence of paid work.
The **appeals handbook** keeps her current team useful while she plans ahead.

steps.text: Finish the insurance appeals handbook with new clerks
Transfer 100 monthly into a separate work-change account

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect my clerk wage to go before I can build another path. Written severance terms, income help, and a funded complaints place with paid hours would give Leila and me something real to plan around.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Please ask insurers whether a person gets paid time to check machine refusals. A customer who has lost a roof needs an answer, not a line that says the software is usually right.

headlineQuote: A customer who has lost a roof needs an answer, not a line that says the software is usually right.
portrait: At 27, Yara leads **disputed claims** at Marlow Mutual and trusts her own careful reading.
She has **three months saved** and shares flat costs with her partner Leila.
She resists new tools, yet seeks **paid appeals work** when jobs and hours look exposed.
Five years buys **paid shadowing**; two years makes her expect lost wages and broken sleep.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her senior clerk post before she can replace the wage.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written redundancy terms**, income help and funded complaints work with paid hours.
